channel.title: Tangle - the good parts
channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The failed impeachment of Pete Hegseth.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, how will congressional Republicans handle being in the minority?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The failed impeachment of Pete Hegseth. On Tuesday, the House voted 211–204 to refer eight articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee. The Republican-controlled committee is not expected to take further action, effectively ending the impeachment attempt. 11 Democrats were absent from the vote, which allowed Republicans to pass the referral measure and avoid a floor vote on impeachment. 

Back up: Impeachment is the process through which Congress can remove certain members of the executive and judicial branches from office. First, a simple majority in the House must vote to impeach. Representatives’ impeachment motions can be referred to committees for further investigation, review, and debate before returning to the House floor for a vote. If the House votes to impeach, the Senate can hold a trial and remove the official from office with a two-thirds majority vote. However, the committee can also choose not to take action. The most recent impeachment of a Cabinet member was President Joe Biden’s Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024; the Senate dismissed those charges. 

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) filed the impeachment resolution. Articles I through III accused Hegseth of illegally launching and continuing the Iran War. Article IV alleged Hegseth ignored laws that are designed to minimize civilian casualties in his decisions on Iran. Article V argued that U.S. strikes against alleged drug boats constituted extrajudicial killings. Article VI accused Hegseth of using his office to suppress Sen. Mark Kelly’s (D-AZ) free speech. Article VII concerned the extradition of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, alleging that it was an illegal kidnapping. Article VIII accused Hegseth of starting an illegal war in Yemen.

Republican leadership originally worried that the impeachment would advance due to poor attendance among their party. However, the House GOP ultimately had fewer absences than Democrats after several members said they missed the vote due to a traffic incident around the Capitol building. 

Democratic leaders have not said whether they will attempt to impeach Hegseth again in 2027, after large House and Senate Democratic majorities will be sworn in. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (NY) did not commit to any action. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said. 

Many Republicans celebrated the result of the vote. “Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” President Donald Trump said. “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”

Today, we’ll share perspectives from the left and right on the attempt to impeach Hegseth. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left supports Hegseth’s impeachment, with some doubting his defense.
  • Many criticize Massie’s strategy in drafting the articles of impeachment. 
  • Others expect Trump to stand by Hegseth for the time being.

In The Intercept, Nick Turse argued “none of it is true.”

“Over half an hour, [Hegseth] declared every military operation he has overseen ‘lawful’ and claims of civilian harm ‘slander.’ He said the Iran war was a great victory and only 18 Americans have died in the conflict. He also claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just ‘one disgruntled congressman,’” Turse said. “Experts in the laws of war, a Pentagon official, and members of Congress from both parties say Hegseth’s boat strikes against ‘cartels,’ which have now killed upward of 240 people, are illegal extrajudicial killings.”

“Of the Iran war, Air Force Lt. Col. Rachel VanLandingham, a former chief of international law at U.S. Central Command, said the opening strike ‘clearly violates the U.S. Constitution and the War Powers Resolution,’” Turse wrote. “The American people, writ large, appear to agree with Ansari, Massie, the U.S. officials, and those in the military’s orbit. Just 32 percent of voters approve of the way Hegseth is handling his job, while 57 percent disapprove.”

In Slate, Jim Newell wrote about “how Pete Hegseth escaped.”

“Hegseth may have been the ripest political target for impeachment. But these articles weren’t written to maximize votes,” Newell said. “Most Republicans have issues with Hegseth… [but] don’t have a problem with what Hegseth has done in Venezuela, or Yemen, or to people in the Caribbean, or his creative interpretations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Most of them support most of that. 

“And even though many don’t like that they lost their elections over high gas and other input prices sparked by the Iran war, they’re not outright opposed to confronting Iran,” Newell wrote. “Massie was asking them not merely to impeach Hegseth; he was asking them to reject the foreign policy of Trump’s first two years. They weren’t about to take that leap on either the policy or the politics. Even retiring members.”

In CNN, Stephen Collinson suggested “Trump is defending himself.”

“Deep into President Donald Trump’s news conference Monday, it became obvious why he’s so adamant in backing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth amid an impeachment storm,” Collinson said. “To jettison the former Fox News anchor now would be to admit that the Iran war — of which Hegseth is the administration’s most vehement proponent — was a mistake. A sacking would also undermine Trump’s attempt to recast what is at best an inconclusive military adventure and at worst a strategic disaster.” 

“If Trump rejected the man who rebranded the Pentagon the ‘Department of War,’ he’d be trashing his own brand,” Collinson wrote. “[Hegseth] seems safe from being ejected from office in the short term, since a two-thirds majority to convict seems unlikely in any Senate impeachment trial… [But] Hegseth could prove to be a liability when Trump needs to get defense spending requests through a Democratic Congress.”

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right question the legitimacy of the articles of impeachment.
  • Some suggest Trump might have turned on Hegseth if he hadn’t been targeted. 
  • Others argue that Hegseth is a political liability.

In Townhall, Horace Cooper said “the impeachment circus comes for the Pentagon.”

“The Framers designed impeachment as an emergency safeguard against treason, bribery, and personal corruption — not as a parliamentary vote of no confidence when lawmakers dislike a president’s foreign policy,” Cooper wrote. “Massie’s resolution… If Congress believes the executive branch has overstepped its constitutional bounds in Iran or the Caribbean, the Constitution already gives lawmakers a decisive, unambiguous tool: the power of the purse.” 

“What Congress should not do is scapegoat a subordinate Cabinet secretary for following lawful directives issued by the elected Commander in Chief,” Cooper said. “Oversight is a vital congressional duty. But turning constitutional impeachment into a tool for lame-duck political theater weakens the presidency, undermines civilian control of the military, and invites endless partisan retaliation the next time power changes hands.”

In The Free Press, Eli Lake asked “did the impeachment threat just save Pete Hegseth?”

“Normally, the prospect of a cabinet secretary’s impeachment would be a reason for a president to cut him loose. In the case of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the threat of impeachment is one very big reason why he will stay in his post at the Pentagon, at least for now,” Lake wrote. “Defending Hegseth makes sense from a political standpoint… Seven of the eight articles in Massie’s impeachment bill directly implicate the president.”

“The irony is that, without the impeachment, Trump and his allies may have found it more convenient to cut Hegseth loose at this point in his term,” Lake said. “The lasting effect of the impeachment gambit may be pushing Trump to defend a member of his cabinet associated with an unpopular war that a segment of his base deeply opposes. Massie has forced the president’s hand and, at least for now, Hegseth will likely survive because of it.”

In The American Conservative, Jude Russo made a “political argument against Pete Hegseth.”

“Let us remember that Hegseth has not been an optimally competent and PR-neutral official, even before he started howling for blood on live television. His Defense Department has been a staffing clown-show, largely self-inflicted; his high-profile reprisals against staffers, some of whom were his longtime friends and allies, in the end turned on entirely baseless accusations of leaking,” Russo wrote. “Hegseth has been a liability machine from the start.”

“Why not pin this stupendously unpopular, difficult to resolve war on him? This is obviously an argument of expediency, not justice (mostly),” Russo said. “There is an endangered official very publicly attached to a very unpopular policy. The president is no stranger to writing off distressed assets. Why not Hegseth? By his own admission, the war is why the GOP lost midterms… It should be underlined that this need not change policy; even a boring secretary of defense will do what he is told to do from on high.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • The past week has brought Democrats back to Earth after their historic midterm performance.
  • The absent Democrats’ excuses don’t add up, and their colleagues are right to be furious. 
  • I’m unsure if Hegseth deserved impeachment, but I think the process would have forced him to be more transparent and accountable.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Welp, the honeymoon is over.

Nine days ago, Democrats were basking in the glow of sweeping electoral fortunes that only come along once or twice in a lifetime. Now it’s back to reality.

Consider what’s happened since last Tuesday’s “blue tsunami.” President Trump tapped Stephen Miller as his chief of staff, the clearest signal yet that he’ll double down on maximizing executive power and lean into culture wars with the left. A few days later, House Republicans tapped Rep. Jim Jordan (OH) to replace House Speaker Mike Johnson (LA) and be their minority leader in the next Congress. Jordan has a near-zero record of passing legislation or whipping votes for leadership (his talent has been organizing votes against leadership), and he’s best known for combative hearings, dressing down Democrats in public, and punchy TV hits. Like the Miller appointment, this is a true “wartime” pick akin to replacing Sherlock Holmes with Jack Reacher. 

Meanwhile, Republicans in the Senate approved a “sense of conference” resolution that pledges to maximize their remaining days in power, attempt to pass another reconciliation bill in the lame duck session, and confirm every judicial nominee and executive nominee they can before January 3 (Republican voters might be wondering where that energy was over the last few months). The White House counsel then sent an overt threat to incoming Democrats that pursuing investigations targeting the Trump administration could be considered criminal, an assertion equaled in its boldness only by its ridiculousness. Trump also scored a major 8–1 win at the Supreme Court, which cleared his administration to continue border wall construction in West Texas, a reminder for Texas Democrats that their wins last week can’t make all their problems disappear.

And how are Democrats wielding their incoming power? Well, on Tuesday Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) argued that if Sen. Chuck Schumer runs unopposed for majority leader, Democrats should withhold quorum and deny the caucus enough members to hold its leadership vote until he presents a clear plan for the path forward with members’ input. That’s probably music to the ears of many Democratic voters who want fresh leadership, but it’s also a reminder that plenty of intraparty battles are around the corner despite the sizable majorities Democrats will enjoy next year.

Which brings us to the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote.

This was Democrats’ first post-midterm opportunity to hold the administration’s feet to the fire, and they really couldn’t have picked a better foil. The Democratic base despises Hegseth. Not to mention, he has drawn harsh criticism from former Defense secretaries and members of the military across party lines. He’s the face of a deeply unpopular war. He is openly loathed by several sitting Republican senators. He’s defended extrajudicial boat strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific that have plausibly killed innocent people. And he was facing articles of impeachment that were brought by a Republican member of Congress. 

Politically, this should have been a layup: I have argued since he was nominated that Hegseth was one of Trump’s worst cabinet picks, an underqualified leader who has a track record of controversy and poor management. I believe his tenure has affirmed that view. Regardless of whether you think impeachment is justified, demanding greater transparency and accountability about the status of the Iran war, the boat strikes, and other conflicts abroad all feel in-bounds to me. I was hoping to see him face some scrutiny.

Of course, given Hegseth’s record, more Republicans than just Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) should have been willing to advance these articles. But all Democrats had to do was show up for the vote, advance the articles of impeachment, and set up weeks of public hearings and media attention on one of the Trump administration’s least popular and most vulnerable Cabinet members — and then, maybe, the Senate would vote to remove him, a historic rebuke.

Yet they couldn’t manage the most basic function of their job.

11 Democrats (and seven Republicans) missed the vote, allowing a successful motion to refer the articles to the House Judiciary Committee and effectively killing the effort until the new Congress convenes. The absentees included some notable figures like Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-CA), once considered the most shrewd operator in the House, whose staff said she was in California receiving a lifetime achievement award (congratulations, I guess?). Also absent was Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI), who became a household name a couple of weeks ago after endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race (she hasn’t explained the absence, but reportedly spent the day before hiding out in the Republican cloakroom). 

Reps. Jonathan Jackson (D-IL), Melanie Stansbury (D-NM), Laura Gillen (D-NY), Marilyn Strickland (D-WA), and Brittany Pettersen (D-CO) each claimed that they missed the vote because of a D.C. traffic jam, which would have been a pretty mediocre excuse on its own. 

Yet it turns out that at least Rep. Jackson was lying. 

TMZ reporter Charlie Cotton saw Jackson on the Capitol steps recording a social media video about Hegseth’s impeachment while the vote was happening, a series of events that sums up this moment in history better than anything I could write here. When Don Lemon confronted Jackson with the timeline, the representative conceded that he had made a mistake, messed up his times, and would take accountability for his actions. Inspiring stuff.

Meanwhile, the Democrats who moved heaven and earth to be there were rightfully infuriated. Rep. Pat Ryan (D-NY) underwent back surgery on Monday and checked himself out of the hospital on Tuesday morning to make the vote. A seething Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA) told MeidasTouch Network on Tuesday night that Democrats “should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.” By Wednesday morning, according to The New York Times, Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-MA) was lambasting party members in a closed-door meeting for squandering the opportunity.

One way to read the last 10 years of U.S. politics is that Donald Trump was elected in 2016 to burn down the status quo. By 2020, voters realized they didn’t much like the alternative and turned to elder statesman Joe Biden to guide the U.S. out of the pandemic. His stewardship produced some very unpopular economic outcomes, which allowed Trump to pull off a remarkable political comeback in 2024. Now, two years into his second term, it appears Americans are remembering what it’s like living under his leadership and not much liking that, either. So once again, voters are wielding their power — and we just got a crystal-clear reminder of how a president can suffer a devastating rebuke of his leadership even while the opposition party remains historically unpopular. 

Democrats were just handed a generational opportunity to rebuild their coalition. That doesn’t start in January — it started this week. And if it’s true that you never get a second chance to make a first impression, the party is already playing from behind with the American public.

Take the survey: Do you think Hegseth will eventually be impeached? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

Under the radar.

This week, the Associated Press reported that 1,156 schools closed during the last academic year, the highest total since the Covid-19 pandemic. The closures come as student enrollment numbers fall, suggesting schools could continue to shut down at an accelerated rate in the years ahead. Researchers say that the decreasing U.S. birth rate is primarily driving the enrollment decline, but recent immigration crackdowns, increased adoption of private school vouchers, and homeschooling are also contributing. Two research groups have estimated that public schools could lose $11.5 billion in annual state revenue by 2030–2031 if enrollment trends continue. The Associated Press has the story.

item.title: Trump says U.S. will end Israel aid.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, how Veterans Day came to be.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

U.S. aid to Israel. On Tuesday, November 3, President Donald Trump announced that U.S. aid to Israel will end at the start of 2027, saying that the country “no longer need[s] it.” The president said that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu brought the idea to him years ago, and the two agreed that now is the time to end the assistance. While Trump indicated that the roughly $3.8 billion in annual aid would be reduced to zero, recent reporting from Israeli outlets suggests the package will only be halved as a result of shortening its time frame. 

Back up: The United States has provided Israel with approximately $300 billion in combined economic and military aid since Israel’s founding. As part of that assistance, the Obama administration signed a memorandum of understanding in 2016, agreeing to send $3.8 billion annually through 2028. The majority of the aid goes to purchases of U.S. military equipment and services; weapons sales are subject to Congressional review, but Congress has never blocked a transfer. 

In his comments on Tuesday, President Trump suggested that the annual aid payments were an effective political target for the left. “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen,” he said. “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like [Democratic Senate candidate Abdul] El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” 

In January, Prime Minister Netanyahu said he wanted to “taper off” U.S. aid to Israel in the next decade. On Friday, he said Trump’s decision to end the annual assistance “shows the strength” of the relationship, adding, “Israel has a strong and stable economy.” 

While President Trump suggested that the aid would end in its entirety in 2027, Israeli news outlets Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported this week that a new memorandum of understanding would continue the aid for five years through 2033, after which it would be phased out completely. The White House has not shared further details on the plan. 

The developments come as political leaders in both parties have scrutinized the U.S.–Israel relationship amid protracted conflicts in the Middle East, including Gaza and Iran. Today, we’ll share views from the right, left, and Israeli writers on the potential aid cutoff. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take. 

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right question when the aid cut will be implemented.
  • Others say the decision won’t change progressives’ criticism of Israel.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board said the leaders “discussed phasing it out over years, not months.”

“President Trump’s Election Day surprise that he will end aid to Israel is less and more than meets the eye. Less because he is acting on a proposal of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and joint plans that have been in the works for at least a year. More because of what the move says about the worsening politics of the U.S.–Israel relationship,” the board wrote. “Mr. Trump came around to the Netanyahu idea; if Israel no longer wanted aid, why force it?

“Discussions advanced to phase out the aid over several years, starting at the end of 2026. That’s why the President’s statement on Tuesday that it would all end in two months caught Israelis unaware. Did Mr. Trump misstate the point? Or did he deliberately put it in the way he felt would be most politically advantageous?” the board asked. “This augurs poorly for the Jewish state, even if it would rather tear off the Band-Aid with Mr. Trump… than have a hostile Democratic President end aid as punishment after 2028.”

In National Review, Noah Rothman suggested “cutting off Israel won’t appease the ‘anti-Zionist’ left.”

“The president’s approach to this issue has a domestic political component. ‘Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like [Abdul] El-Sayed when they don’t need it?’ Trump asked. ‘It’s a bad talking point,’” Rothman wrote. “If this becomes U.S. policy at the beginning of next year, as Trump forecast, it will have about as much effect on the anti-Israel left’s advocacy as did the end of high-tempo combat operations inside Gaza 13 months ago. Which is to say, it won’t have any effect at all.”

“Those who continue to rail against the ongoing ‘genocide’ inside Gaza are operating independently of the facts on the ground. Why should an amendment to a line item that consumes 0.05% of America’s annual outlays represent a moderating force?” Rothman asked. “There are many compelling reasons to transition away from the current posture toward Israel on which both sides of the equation can agree. But mollifying Israel’s monomaniacal critics isn’t one of them. They cannot be appeased.”

What the left is saying.
  • Some on the left suggest the political costs of aid aren’t worth it for Israel.
  • Others say the U.S.’s relationship with Israel is evolving.

In Vox, Eric Levitz wrote about “the Israeli case against U.S. aid to Israel.”

“Trump’s remarks Tuesday morning seem to have been ad-libbed. The Israeli Treasury Department reportedly had no knowledge of a supposed joint agreement to end U.S. aid. And existing U.S. law provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual funding through 2028. All this said, Trump didn’t pluck his Election Day rant out of thin air,” Levitz wrote. “Rather, his remarks actually reflect a prominent strain of thinking among Israeli leaders and security experts. 

“In their view, America’s cash may no longer be worth the political blowback that it invites,” Levitz said. “A voter doesn’t need to have any strong opinion about the Israel–Palestine conflict to oppose sending billions of dollars to a wealthy foreign country… On the U.S. left, right, and center, political winds are blowing against aid to Israel. With some of that country’s own leaders and admirers bowing to such gusts, the draw down of American aid to Israel might now be a matter of when, not if.”

In MS NOW, Zeeshan Aleem said “the foreign policy script is flipping.”

“Trump remains under fire for joining forces with Israel in an unpopular war with Iran, and his Tuesday statement sounded like a Hail Mary attempt to help the GOP win over swing voters who oppose aid to the U.S. ally,” Aleem wrote. “If that particular aid package is ended, it’s likely to be replaced by a more covert policy of arming Israel with U.S. weapons. But Trump clearly recognized that it could be politically advantageous to appear to be severing aid to Israel. 

“A slow-moving but seismic shift is taking place across American politics: Progressives are gaining real power in the debate over Israel,” Aleem said. “For decades, the conventional wisdom has held that criticizing Israel too forcefully is politically lethal. But Trump saw an Arab American progressive like El-Sayed as a threat to the GOP’s voter base because he criticized Israel. We seem to be in the early stages of an inversion of the bipartisan consensus on support for the longtime ally.”

What Israeli writers are saying.
  • Many Israeli writers note that aiding Israel also benefited the U.S.
  • Others say Israeli leaders must better justify the decision to end the assistance.

In JNS, Duvi Honig suggested “aid to Israel was also Israel’s aid to America.”

“U.S. President Donald Trump’s announcement about ending approximately $4 billion in annual U.S. military aid to Israel has people worried, as though Israel just suffered a terrible financial loss,” Honig wrote. “My reaction is exactly the opposite: Thank You, Hashem! It’s all for the best. For decades, Israel has been giving America extraordinary strategic, technological, intelligence and economic value while being portrayed as the country standing with its hand out.” 

“How much has American research and development benefited from Israeli expertise? How many American lives and military resources have been protected through Israeli intelligence and defense technology?” Honig asked. “Perhaps what looks like a financial loss will become the beginning of greater economic independence, more opportunities for Israeli industries and a partnership that better recognizes Israel’s true contributions.”

In The Jerusalem Post, Yoram Dori called the aid “a central pillar of Israel’s national security and military planning.”

“Let us consider the facts. American military assistance is not some generous Christmas present that Israel can politely decline,” Dori wrote. “Ending that assistance prematurely would represent a serious blow to Israel’s defense capabilities and impose an enormous additional burden on Israeli taxpayers… The American assistance agreement is not merely a financial arrangement. It reflects a long-standing bipartisan commitment to Israel’s security. 

“For decades, Israeli leaders understood that maintaining bipartisan American support was a strategic national interest, not a partisan luxury,” Dori said. “Let the transitional prime minister publish the terms of the deal. Let him explain why Israel should surrender nearly $4 billion annually, what strategic advantages Israel will receive, and how the resulting gap in our defense budget will be filled. And, above all, let him explain why this extraordinary announcement had to be made on the very day Americans went to the polls.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • The debate over U.S. aid to Israel is clouded by misunderstandings about what the relationship actually entails. 
  • The aid offers mutual benefits — and it comes with important conditions. 
  • I’m not inherently opposed to ending the assistance, but it could result in some unintended consequences.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

For a long time, I’ve sensed a fundamental contradiction in the way Americans discuss our aid to Israel.

Casual political observers, anti-Israel activists, and — frankly — antisemites all tend to portray Israel as entirely dependent on the United States for its survival, yet somehow powerful enough to dictate American foreign policy. In this framing, Israel is both a beggar that needs the U.S. to survive in the Middle East and an all-powerful puppet master that pulls the strings of U.S. policy. It’s rather absurd if you think about it for a moment.

In reality, and in a stroke of irony, the most zealous Zionists in Israel have long wanted the same thing progressive, pro-Palestine voters in America want: to wean Israel from U.S. aid. For the Israeli right, no longer taking money from America would mean no longer having to explain their actions to a Western government and populace that don’t understand how a fundamentally non-Western country must operate to live in safety in the Middle East. The United States is not the only place Israel can buy weapons from, and the chance to shed the often constrictive rules of American foreign aid is highly desirable to many Israelis.

A lot of Americans (and, apparently, some American journalists who write about Israel) don’t seem to grasp that Israel is not a Western country. It is not a little America. It is not Europe. It is Middle Eastern, through and through. Our relationship with Israel is less akin to an allyship with France or Canada than it is to Egypt or India. Israel is just different from America. 

It’s worth being specific about what aid to Israel actually comprises. Some frame it as “giving” Israel $3.8 billion a year, while others suggest Israel is just buying $3.8 billion of U.S. weapons. The reality sits somewhere in between: It’s a grant of U.S. taxpayer money that goes to Israel, which must be mostly spent on American weapons and military technology. In other words, this is not a loan — the U.S. government doesn’t get the money back — but Israel spends the bulk of the funds on deals with American defense contractors like Lockheed Martin or Boeing.

The Israel aid does have some unique elements: For one, it’s a lot of money. While defenders of U.S. aid often note that $38 billion over ten years is just 0.05% of the federal budget, $3.8 billion a year is far more military aid than any other country gets from the U.S. in a normal year. The next closest is Ukraine ($1.0 billion a year) and then Jordan ($429 million a year).

Second, Israel aid has two special conditions that make it unique: It can use the funding to purchase arms from its own domestic industry (in FY2024, it was allowed to use roughly $770 million on buying Israeli arms). Also, the U.S. sends the funds to an account with the U.S. Federal Reserve, so the Israeli government benefits from the interest on those funds (many other countries receiving U.S. foreign aid draw funds as they are needed). 

This kind of “special” arrangement has long been a bedrock of American–Israeli relations. And in a lot of ways it makes sense: The Middle East is a hostile region for the United States, so allies there are at a premium (this is, incidentally, why Egypt and Jordan are also top recipients of U.S. funding — though that gets far less attention). Intelligence sharing, technological exchange, and some values alignment (like a free press, democracy, and independent courts) make Israel incredibly valuable to us for a relatively small cost. Israel also regularly limits the growing power of our mutual adversaries (like Iran).

There’s also the more organic crossover: Most population estimates find that only Canada, the United Kingdom, Mexico, and France have more Americans living in their countries than Israel. And as a proportion of the population, nobody is close: Even low-end estimates of 200,000 Americans in Israel would mean roughly 2% of the 10 million-person population is American (compared to roughly 0.64% to 1.1% of people living in Canada). The simple reality is that many Americans living in Israel create all manner of incentives to grow military, political, financial, and even spiritual bonds.

These entanglements are, again, a core part of the relationship that is often overlooked by the people who view Israel as a kind of leech on American power and cash. It’s reasonable to argue that Israel provides just as much as it takes from the United States. And far from being the orchestrator of American politics, the Israel lobby — the all-powerful Jewish overlords — actually fails to get what it wants from America on a regular basis. In a debate with the anti-Israel comic Dave Smith, writer and podcaster Coleman Hughes recently listed examples of requests that Israel failed to get from past United States presidents, including decades of not recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights and decades of not moving the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem, among others. Interestingly, it’s been President Trump — the man now proposing aid cuts — who has seemed to be most amenable to the Israel lobby: He eventually did recognize Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights (in 2019) and moved the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem (in 2018). He also tore up the Obama administration’s nuclear deal with Iran and followed Netanyahu into the Iran war.

Yet even Trump doesn’t always give what the lobby wants: He lifted sanctions on Syria against the Israeli government’s wishes, orchestrated a truce with Houthi rebels in Yemen without forcing them to stop firing on Israel, and even struck a hostage deal with Hamas without involving Israeli negotiators. That’s to say nothing of all the money the Israel lobby regularly wastes failing to defeat candidates it views as hostile toward Israel (this recent election being a notable example). 

Given all this, I’m not sure the people calling for an end to U.S. aid to Israel have a genuine grasp of the more far-reaching consequences. Our relationship with Israel is a constant push and pull — one that undergoes changes every decade. Not giving Israel money to buy American weapons is not the same as not supporting Israel in its wars in Gaza, Lebanon, or Iran. In fact, the money we do grant Israel is one key leverage point deployable to sway its behavior. So if you want Israel to more closely align itself with American values, or to be more responsive to sentiment from American voters, cutting off its aid is not very tactical.

In some ways, I’m almost hopeful that Trump follows through on his promise so Americans can see clearly that shaping a foreign nation’s actions is not as simple as cutting off grants for it to buy our weapons. America has long functioned as a restraint on leaders like Benjamin Netanyahu, and it’s a good thing those restraints have existed. So for the people who feel like their wishes are finally coming true, I might remember the old maxim to be careful what you wish for. 

Take the survey: What do you think of the U.S. potentially ending aid to Israel? Let us know. 

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff.
item.dc:creator: Carina Pacheco
item.description: Plus, did Democrats run “decent” campaigns in 2026?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

Stephen Miller as chief of staff. On Friday, President Donald Trump announced he is elevating Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff, while current Chief of Staff Susie Wiles will move to a position in the “Trump Political Operation.” The move is one of the White House’s first major personnel changes following last week’s midterm elections. 

Back up: Miller, 41, previously served as a deputy chief of staff in the second Trump administration, focusing primarily on the president’s mass deportation effort, anti-fraud initiatives, and military operations against alleged drug traffickers. He has been a top adviser to Trump since his first administration and earned a reputation for hard-line immigration views. 

Wiles reportedly resigned on Thursday. She managed President Trump’s 2024 campaign and is his longest-serving White House chief of staff across his two administrations. In a statement, she said serving as chief of staff was “the honor of a lifetime.” 

As the architect of the White House’s immigration policy, Miller has set aggressive goals for deportations and sought to leverage executive authority to expedite removals of alleged noncitizens. Those efforts have drawn a litany of legal challenges and some rulings restraining the administration’s actions. 

On X, Miller said, “I am honored beyond words to serve as [Trump’s] White House Chief of Staff,” adding, “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.”

Some Republicans praised the move, including House Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-MD), who said, “Stephen Miller has built a proven record focused on securing our border, combating crime, and advancing a now much-needed common-sense conservative agenda for our country.” Others questioned the decision; outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) called it “a colossal mistake” after Republicans’ midterm losses. 

Democrats criticized Miller’s promotion; Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, said, “Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families. Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct.” 

Below are views from the left and right on the pick. Then, Associate Editor Carina Pacheco’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left criticizes the move, saying Miller’s elevation is Trump doubling down on his most controversial initiatives. 
  • Some suggest Miller’s promotion signals the administration will lean further into its hard-line immigration agenda. 
  • Others argue Republican politicians should oppose Miller’s promotion.

In Slate, Ian Prasad Philbrick asked “did Trump learn anything from the midterms?”

“It isn’t unusual for presidents to reshuffle the org chart after a midterm drubbing. But those personnel changes are usually a tacit admission that something has gone wrong, a public hitting of the reset button,” Philbrick wrote. “[Trump] has never cared much for the will of the voters. And promoting Miller, who is among the administration’s most despised figures, is the opposite of what most presidents would do after an overwhelming electoral beatdown.”

“Promoting Miller starts to make more sense when you consider who Trump is at his core: a confrontational man who managed to get elected president twice in large part by stoking divisions over immigration,” Philbrick said. “Ever in search of a scapegoat for his own failures, Trump has reportedly blamed Republicans’ hefty midterm losses on Susie Wiles… And rather than confront the reality of defeat, Trump appears to be seeking succor among his core supporters.”

In New York Magazine, Ed Kilgore called Miller’s promotion “a chilling sign for [the] final Trump years.”

“Putting Miller into her place is a pretty clear signal of defiance to Democrats, to Republicans who wanted a change of direction, and to the electorate,” Kilgore wrote. “Miller is deeply responsible for losing 2024 Trump voters who supported border control and deportation of violent criminals but never bargained for the terror ICE has inflicted on immigrant communities or the unapologetic racism that underlies Miller’s approach to immigration.

“And that may be the scariest thing of all about his new base of power: He has two more years to act on his deep belief in the Great Replacement Theory. This is the idea that traitorous liberals are deliberately destroying the country through a conspiracy to drown native white Americans in a sea of shiftless immigrants who trade illegal votes for welfare benefits and the opportunity to commit crimes,” Kilgore said. “Trump talks about this nightmare scenario all the time as part of his demagogic pitch to the MAGA base. But for Miller, it’s an article of faith.”

In Bloomberg, Erika D. Smith argued “Stephen Miller is not what voters asked for.”

“Trump has obviously learned nothing from the worst political shellacking in a half-century. Promoting Miller is the clearest sign yet that the president plans to approach his last two years in office much like his first two — pursuing deeply unpopular policies, regardless of what most voters want,” Smith wrote. “Trump wanted a chief of staff who ‘will crack skulls,’ as a source familiar with the decision told the Atlantic, because he ‘doesn’t want to be reined in.’ Republicans, just for their own political survival, would be foolish to go along with that.”

“Republicans might be tempted to shrug this off, figuring that voters care more about high prices for gas, groceries and housing than they do about immigrants being hauled away by federal agents,” Smith said. “But that doesn’t mean voters don’t care about immigration. Or that Miller’s style of hardline enforcement won’t undermine their support for the Republican Party.”

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right suggest Miller is a high-risk, high-reward chief of staff.
  • Others say he’s well equipped to push Trump’s agenda forward. 
  • Still others worry his confrontational tactics will be counterproductive.

The New York Post editorial board wrote “Trump goes to the mattresses with Stephen Miller.”

“[Wiles] was crucial to President Donald Trump’s return to the Oval Office and the excellent start to his second term. You could not ask for a more loyal gatekeeper — one dedicated to forwarding Trump’s core agenda without pride or prejudice — nor a hand more deft at balancing attack and defense, conflict and cooperation,” the board said. “News that she’ll be replaced by Stephen Miller removes almost all hope that the nation’s partisan warfare will ease after the elections.”

“The president is circling the wagons in a way that’s likely to leave a lot of potential allies on the outside. It also signals that Trump has decided that he wants to appeal to his shrinking base, rather than attempt to rebuild the wider coalition that swept him to power but soundly rejected him and his party this week,” the board wrote. “The coming spectacle will be more bloody than a cage fight on the White House lawn.”

In RedState, Brandon Morse called Miller “a wartime consigliere.”

“The Left hope[d] the Republicans put up a well-informed, professional-sounding, and ultimately boring guy. Miller is not that,” Morse said. “Miller has the ability to give info and make it look like fireworks are going off. You enjoy watching him beat people over the head with facts. He’s on the offensive and knows how to make a jab sound professional… If Trump is going to keep his administration going as strongly as he can, he’s going to need to bring these kinds of people to the forefront.

“[Trump] is at war. To be clear, he always has been, but after the midterms, he’s now on the losing side. His PR isn’t exactly going well, so he needs competent fighters. I think Miller absolutely qualifies as one of the best,” Morse wrote. “The more [Miller is] in front of a camera the more defensively the Left has to play, and the more defense they have, the better it looks for Republicans.”

In National Review, Mark Antonio Wright argued “Miller will double down on Trumpism.”

“Miller’s extreme performative combativeness — even when defending what should be defensible policy positions — is not always helpful to the administration he serves,” Wright said. “He usually comes off indignant, heated, and like he’s trying to win a debating point in whatever the argument is of that moment; there seems to be little thought to strategically advancing the ball down the field more generally.”

“Expect Stephen Miller to double down on Trumpism. That may or may not bring the Trump administration wins on policy. It may or may not be an effective strategy to delay, distract, and defuse Democratic congressional investigations into the administration’s actions and potential corruption,” Wright wrote. “But just don’t expect the Trump administration’s actions under Miller’s influence to suddenly become politically popular. The track record, in fact, points to the opposite as the most likely outcome.”

My take.
Carina Pacheco
Associate Editor
 
  • Trump is rewarding Miller despite Miller’s responsibility for the policies that have made Republicans so unpopular.
  • His promotion expedites the fracturing of the GOP.
  • Trump wants a loyal fighter in his corner, but Miller will exacerbate the issues that led to the midterm losses.

More than anything else, last week’s “blue tsunami” was a rejection of the second Trump administration. Afterward, the president took a surprisingly chastened tone — he said he’s open to working with Democrats and doesn’t want to spend his final two years in office vetoing everything a Democratic Congress passes. Sure, he’s dabbled in election fraud claims and seems unwilling to reckon with the role he played in his party’s midterm defeat. But overall, his immediate response was muted. 

Appointing Stephen Miller as chief of staff, though, hits a completely different note. 

Politico reported that some Republicans shared my reaction to the news, writing: “One House Republican, when informed that Trump had named Miller his chief of staff, replied: ‘Please tell me you’re lying to me right now, just to get a reaction.’” This unnamed official is not alone in their distress at the appointment; Republicans are trying to discern what a Trump-less future looks like, and Miller’s promotion complicates that picture. It all but ensures that some of the most polarizing policies of Trump’s tenure will continue to be center stage in his final years in office. 

As the New York Post editorial board said (in “What the right is saying”), Trump is circling the wagons around the policies that cost Republicans control of Congress; and, in my view, he’s expediting the fracturing of the party. For all the handwringing about whether or not Trumpism or MAGA is dead, Miller is the guy fighting tooth and nail to keep it alive. 

Miller has been building up to this moment since his youth. As a teenager, he played provocateur on Larry Elder’s radio show by complaining about the left-wing culture of his Santa Monica high school and the rising prominence of political correctness. While at Duke University, Miller spoke out against what he viewed as left-wing institutional bias, explored polarizing topics in his opinion column in The Duke Chronicle, and backed the defendants in the 2006 Duke lacrosse scandal, who he believed were presumed guilty due to their race and socioeconomic status (the case fell apart, and he was vindicated). Since he was a young man, Miller has reveled in any opportunity to wade into the culture wars. 

Wall Street Journal editor Zachary Kessel observed that if Susie Wiles represented the restrained version of Trump, Miller is maximalist Trump. Politically, he is synonymous with aggressive immigration policies and appears to relish his role as a zealous firebrand promoting the right’s more extreme political positions. Miller goes much further than many in his party with vitriolic nativist rhetoric. He embodies the cognitive dissonance of “America is for Americans and Americans only” — the United States, after all, is a country unique for its history of immigration and the belief that, in President Ronald Reagan’s words, “anyone, from any corner of the Earth, can come to live in America and become an American.” Miller himself is the descendant of not-so-distant Jewish ancestors.

Yet his worldview centers on threats of foreign “invasion,” the dangers of multiculturalism, and economic challenges created by immigration. While some conservatives and moderates may share these concerns in broad strokes — for example, opposition to open borders and an interest in cultural assimilation — Miller’s existential, militaristic messaging clearly doesn’t resonate. 

In his heart of hearts, I think Miller truly believes extremely limited immigration is the most straightforward way to protect American laws, values and traditions, and that being called a racist and xenophobe is a small price for him to pay in his larger mission. While voters may have appreciated some of those positions in theory, they have now starkly rejected them in practice.

It was Miller’s idea to set daily apprehension quotas and expand enforcement operations for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). It was his idea to restrict H-1B visas for high-skill foreign workers. It was his idea to aggressively target anyone in the country illegally, not just those with criminal records. It was his idea to invoke the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to speed up deportations of alleged foreign gang members. It was his idea to curtail birthright citizenship via executive order. 

While Miller isn’t personally to blame for the war in Iran, inflation, tariffs and Trump family corruption, he is the architect and defender of the kind of hard-line policies voters resoundingly rejected on Tuesday. Trump’s approval rating on immigration, usually his strongest issue, has fallen considerably. Latinos, who secured Trump’s 2024 victory, moved sharply to the left. Even in the border state stronghold of Texas, voters chose a Democrat for both Senator and Governor. Miller-backed Texas railroad commissioner candidate Bo French, who ran on anti-DEI and anti-immigration, also lost his race to a Democrat. All that to say — Trump rewarding Miller with a promotion is either incredibly hubristic, incredibly shortsighted, or both. 

The president seems well aware of why his party got wiped out on Tuesday, and even well aware of the reality that his tough-on-immigration policy hurt him with many voters. He seems preoccupied with cementing his own legacy via construction projects and completely unconcerned by how Republicans will position themselves in 2028. In a 60 Minutes interview that aired last night, the president acknowledged that backlash against his hardline immigration policies contributed to his party’s midterm losses. He even floated the possibility of his steering clear of the 2028 Republican presidential contest, saying, “Maybe I’m better off not getting involved.” So perhaps Miller’s elevation is more of a personal calculation than a political one: a reward for a decade of loyalty and an opportunity to delegate day-to-day decisions to someone he trusts.

Also likely, though, is that Trump wants Miller to keep the base energized and execute his agenda while embodying a take-no-prisoners attitude against a combative Democratic Congress and some very skeptical Republicans. Trump understands that Miller’s views are extreme, but I think he believes someone in this mold will be his best defense against incoming investigations.

Promoting Miller creates an intricate mess for the would-be successors of Trump’s movement, and picks a side in a fight Republicans would probably rather avoid. The MAGA coalition is fracturing in real time on the issues that will partially define the 2028 election — legal immigration versus no immigration, interventionism versus isolationism, and economic populism versus limited government among them. Miller sits at the far end of those divides, and every Republican eyeing 2028 will have to decide whether to stand with him or against him.

Trump can talk about working with Democrats all he likes, but feigning a placatory tone is easy. Choosing to double down on Miller as a prominent voice in his administration is much more complicated and suggests Trump isn’t really as coy about the next two years as he’s letting on; the question is whether his party will pay for it in 2028.

Staff concurrence.
Russell Nystrom
Associate Editor
 
 
In addition to Miller being the engine behind some of the Trump administration’s most controversial policies, he isn’t a “negotiate with Democrats” kind of guy. He’s more of a “govern through executive fiat and move as fast as possible before the court system catches up” person.
 
He’s called the Democratic Party a “domestic extremist organization.” He’s said it is full of “freaks, weirdos, losers, and crazies.” He’s said that Democrats are communists and cowards, and that they want to destroy America. But it goes beyond rhetoric: Every time Miller has been placed in a position to negotiate with Democrats, he’s blown everything up. His positioning has even led to accusations that he intentionally scuttles deals; the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC) once said, “As long as Stephen Miller is in charge of negotiating immigration, we're going nowhere.”
 
None of this suggests Miller is actually capable of reaching compromises with Democrats, who are about to have huge majorities in Congress. What you can expect is more governing through executive orders. At the same time, I’m left with large concerns about how negotiating a budget, a potential debt default, and other must-pass bills will go with Stephen Miller in his new position.
